prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping, which brought atomic timekeeping to the 1e-18 level of accuracy and stability

statement.case_for: I keep optical lattice clocks (B018) as a single two-person part and I do not change my preferred configuration from round 1. After reading the full exchange, the case rests on three things that nobody disputes: the magic-wavelength lattice is a distinct idea that cancels the light shift while holding many atoms free of Doppler and recoil broadening; the resulting 1e-18 performance is measured and has been reproduced and compared in several independent laboratories; and the consequences, from the pending redefinition of the second to relativistic geodesy and searches for varying constants and ultralight dark matter, are already being pursued. The chair's summary records that no member argues B018 is premature or unoriginal, and I treat that as a statement about the science, not as a vote count. I moved to this position from my opening choice (B020) because B018 is the one candidate where I can state the specific discovery in one sentence and name who made which step. That is the standard I would apply to any part I put my name to. The citation should be written narrowly, around the magic-wavelength lattice clock, so that it does not silently claim all of optical timekeeping.
statement.case_against: The strongest argument against is the one Kroll, Lindroth and Olsson each raised against their own first choice: that the lattice step can be read as a refinement of already honoured work (laser cooling 1997, the frequency comb 2005, ion control 2012), and that a prize for measurement precision is metrology rather than a discovery. I do not think that is decisive, because the lattice idea changes what is possible and is not a mere extension of cooling or combs, but I cannot call it settled. The second reservation is attribution by omission: a two-name credit leaves out Lemonde, Ludlow, Bloom, Hinkley and the ion-clock groups, and nobody on the committee, myself included, has verified the priority sequence between the early lattice proposals and the first operating clocks. Third, the redefinition of the second has not yet happened. I would not delay for it, but I acknowledge that a prize on this topic will be read partly in that light. Finally, this is outside my own field of electronic-structure theory, and I am relying on colleagues in atomic physics for the technical claims on systematic uncertainties.

responses.point: Pearce keeps IceCube (B007) as his first choice for Halzen and Karle, arguing that a new messenger and a cubic-kilometre instrument is a discovery, that the diffuse flux beyond 100 TeV is secure, and that source identification is a consequence rather than the basis.
responses.response: I accept the chair's framing that the diffuse flux is the cited achievement, and I accept that a new observational window is the kind of discovery the prize was created for. I also note he acknowledges that credit in a collaboration of hundreds is hard to assign. That is where I stay unconvinced. His own answer to the attribution problem is a two-name compromise (Halzen, Karle) that omits Yoshida, and the AMANDA and Baikal precursors and early concept proponents are still outside it. I would rather defend a clean credit with a contested discovery character than a strong discovery character with a contested credit. I have moved B007 up to my first alternative as a result of the exchange, because I take his point that B018 is a precision advance, but it does not change my lead. If the committee can answer the credit question for IceCube in a way I find defensible, I would reopen it.

responses.point: Kroll keeps B018 first but sets out the strongest objection: lattice clocks may be the sum of laser cooling, the comb and ion control, and he has not independently verified the priority between early lattice proposals and the first clocks.
responses.response: I share both reservations and want to be as explicit as he was. On the first, I think the answer is that cooling, the comb and ion control were necessary tools while the magic-wavelength idea is what makes a many-atom neutral-atom clock work at all, so it is a separate step with its own result, not a reprise. On the second, I agree that this is an open item, and since I cannot verify it from my own field I think the committee should not present the credit as proven. I would answer his question about omission by keeping the citation tied to the magic-wavelength lattice, which describes what Katori and Ye did without pretending to cover the ion clocks or other lattice-clock groups.

responses.point: Johansson keeps Cirac and Zoller (B032) as a theory prize for the proposals behind trapped-ion gates and cold-atom quantum simulation, treating the 2012 prize as experiments recognised separately.
responses.response: The chair's summary shows that his disagreement is with the discovery character, not the science, and I respect that the originality and the clean two-name credit are not in doubt. My concern from round 1 remains: the proposals lean on experimental realisations that are credited elsewhere, and the overlap with B015 (Bloch, Greiner with the same two names) means a B032 prize reaches into a neighbouring achievement under a three-person limit. In the chair's question about whether B032 and B015 are one achievement or two, I think two would be hard to defend and one would force a choice between theory and the experimenters. That leaves B032 below B018 for me, though I would still treat it as a serious option if the committee wants a theory prize.

responses.point: Lindroth supports B018 but wants the citation kept narrow, asks whether a broader optical-clock wording would reach ion-clock pioneers, and discloses that her priority timeline rests on recollection.
responses.response: I agree with the narrow wording and have drafted my citation that way. I disagree that broadening it would improve the credit. A broader optical-clock citation would reach the ion-clock pioneers but would then overlap the 2012 prize and the 2005 prize and would lose the property that makes B018 attractive, that it names one invention and its realisation. I take her recollection caveat seriously and share it: my own knowledge of the sequence is secondhand. The committee should check the early lattice proposals and the first operating clocks before the vote, instead of assuming that the ballots already agree.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers fluctuation theorems and stochastic thermodynamics (B002) for Jarzynski, Evans and Seifert, and stated that no colleague ranked it in the opening.
responses.response: I remain impressed by the conceptual quality and by the experiments from optical tweezers to single-molecule pulling, and I do not question the physics. What the round-1 exchange sharpened for me is that no one, including him, has identified a single result that carries the citation: steady-state fluctuation relation, Jarzynski equality, and trajectory entropy production are different results with different priorities, and Crooks is an omission he himself calls awkward. Until the committee can name one result and three people, I cannot move B002 above B018, but the question the chair put to him is a fair one.

uncertainties: Whether the priority sequence between the early lattice-clock proposals and the first operating clocks supports crediting Katori with the concept and Ye with the accuracy and many-body-limited operation, since no member has verified it.
Whether the committee will see the lattice step as distinct from laser cooling (1997), the frequency comb (2005) and ion control (2012), or as a refinement of them.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second should affect timing. I would not wait, but I cannot rule out that others will.
Whether a two-name IceCube credit can be made defensible. If so, B007 would be the strongest competitor to B018.
Whether the strontium and ytterbium lattice-clock contributors left out of the credit (Lemonde, Ludlow, Bloom, Hinkley) create an attribution problem that the two-name configuration hides.
statement.conflict_note: No personal or institutional conflict with any shortlisted candidate is apparent from my profile. My research field (electronic-structure theory, DFT and DFT+DMFT, magnetism) is close to B020, B003, B034 and B044, which is a methodological bias and not a recusal ground. B018 is outside my field, so I defer to colleagues in atomic physics on its technical claims. I served as Chair for the 2025 cycle, whose prize concerned macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits, and that is relevant only to the perceived proximity of B008, not to B018.
